papers.title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model
papers.abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88). Its predicted variant effects agree with likely causal caQTLs (Spearman correlation = 0.52) but not with variants associated only through linkage, a traditionally challenging task. Overall, ModBERT establishes a framework for personal-genome language modeling, in which a model reads each individual's genetic and epigenetic sequence rather than a shared reference. This enables in silico dissection of variant and methylation effects on gene regulation and principled prioritization of candidates for experimental validation as population-scale long-read cohorts (e.g., 1KGP and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium) grow.

papers.title: Benchmarking DNA foundation models for zero-shot variant effect prediction shows the importance of context, training, and architecture.
papers.abstract: In this study, we systematically evaluate the performance of several DNA foundation models (NT, DNABERT, HyenaDNA and Evo 2) in predicting the functional impact of genetic variants using Zero-shot scoring, a method that does not require task-specific fine-tuning. We assess the models' sensitivity to sequence alterations introduced by Single Nucleotide Variants (SNVs), comparing their ability to capture both local and extended contextual effects. Using pathogenic, benign, and uncertain SNVs from ClinVar, we show that large multi-species NT models outperform other architectures in detecting functional consequences, not only at the SNV site but also in adjacent regions. These models exhibit superior discriminative power across variant categories, especially when aggregating Zero-shot scores over multiple surrounding tokens. Conversely, models trained solely on human sequences or relying on a next-token prediction objective, such as DNABERT, HyenaDNA, and Evo 2, exhibit limited contextual awareness and a reduced ability to differentiate variant effects. Our findings highlight the critical importance of model size, training objective, and training data diversity in shaping model performance. Furthermore, we discuss current limitations in modeling long-range dependencies in genomic sequences and suggest that innovations in transformer architectures, such as sparse attention or memory-augmented models, may provide viable paths toward scalable, genome-wide variant effect prediction.

papers.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
papers.abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

papers.title: DynamicsPLM: A Dynamics-Enriched Small Protein Language Model for Protein Variant Effect Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting how mutations impact protein function and stability remains a key challenge in computational biology. Current state-of-the-art protein language models (PLMs) primarily scale parameter size on sequence corpora to capture evolutionary constraints but remain blind to the explicit physical dynamics of folded proteins. Conversely, models trained strictly on physical dynamics neglect critical evolutionary sequence statistics. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing DynamicsPLM, a highly parameter-efficient 35-million-parameter model that unifies evolutionary and biophysical representation learning. Utilizing a second-stage, multi-task continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins, we enrich a foundational sequence encoder with explicit residue-level and pairwise molecular dynamics heads while preserving its original evolutionary knowledge. At inference, DynamicsPLM computes zero-shot mutation effects from sequence alone by balancing an evolutionary plausibility score against a structural dynamics disruption score. Across the massive ProteinGym benchmark and natural variants of the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, DynamicsPLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among all models under 100M parameters, and matches or outperforms several billion-scale sequence-based models of its size. Our findings demonstrate that explicit structural-dynamics supervision provides a parameter-efficient alternative to raw scale. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations for LoMuS are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/DynamicsPLM.

papers.title: DeePEn - A Depth sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering
papers.abstract: Recent progress in modeling techniques and high-throughput screening has significantly enhanced the accessibility of protein engineering. Nevertheless, further progress gets hindered by the lack of robust benchmarks that capture the practical challenges for real-world protein engineering. Here, we introduced DeePEn, a Depth-sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering that quantifies model generalization to held-out variants at increasing mutational distance from the wild type. We defined distance as the number of simultaneous point mutations, i.e., single amino acid variants (SAVs), moving from wild-type to mutant (edit distance in computer science jargon). DeePEn retrospectively evaluates prediction and prioritization using experimentally labelled variants from deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets; it does not benchmark prospective sequence generation or goal-directed optimization. Specifically selecting four DMS datasets with sufficient multi-mutation data points from ProteinGym, we assessed recent predictive models, including general and biophysics-informed protein Language Models (pLMs), and a non-transformer neural network. Our results highlight how the performance of all models deteriorates with increasing mutational distance and that no single metric sufficiently captures the diverse requirements of protein engineering. To overcome these shortcomings, DeePEn provides a readily available resource for multi-metric benchmarking that focuses on variant-effect prediction of variants distant from the wild type.

papers.title: Single-cell machine learning uncovers genetically anchored, cell-type specific programs of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Univariate differential expression analysis dominates single-cell transcriptomic studies of Alzheimer's disease, yet marginal testing alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure or distinguish clinical from neuropathological signatures. Here we introduce TriSCOPE, a framework integrating multivariate predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression, and pseudotime inference, applied to six Alzheimer's disease snRNA-seq datasets comprising ~4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors. Across six major brain cell types and 41 subclusters, we identify cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that are largely non-overlapping with differentially expressed genes, revealing disease-relevant signals invisible to univariate approaches. Conditional GWAS-eQTL colocalization anchors a subset of these predictively expressed genes to inherited Alzheimer's disease risk loci, including 27 genetically supported gene-cell type pairs (among them ARL17B, JAZF1) with no significant differential expression. Integration across all three analytical branches nominates high-confidence convergent programs including astrocytic stress markers (such as GFAP, MT2A), neuronal signaling genes (like RASGEF1B, LINGO1, NRG1), and microglial and oligodendrocyte regulators (including SYTL3, SPP1, APOD). Comparison of clinical and neuropathological models reveals cell-type-specific divergence between cognitive and pathological Alzheimer's disease signatures. Key predictively expressed genes including ARL17B, LINGO1, and APOE replicate across independent cohorts, with cross-cohort generalizability confirmed across all three analytical branches of TriSCOPE.

papers.title: A Three-Axis Framework for Therapy Prioritization in MBD4-Deficient Tumors: De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Modeling, Replication-Stress Pharmacology, and PARP1 Trapping Decoupling
papers.abstract: Background: Loss-of-function mutations in MBD4 (methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 4) cause a specialized base excision repair (BER) deficiency characterized by hypermutated CpG>TpG signatures and sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade. However, post-immunotherapy treatment prioritization remains empirically unmapped. In clinical oncology, DNA damage response (DDR) defects are frequently extrapolated to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) sensitivity by analogy to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), without testing whether upstream glycosylase loss generates the nicked single-strand break (SSB) intermediates required for toxic PARP1-DNA trapping. Methods: We developed a three-axis framework integrating mechanistic curation, large-scale pharmacogenomics (DepMap 24Q2 CRISPR/RNA-seq, n=1,517; GDSC2 dose-response profiling, n=928; PRISM Repurposing), and a 5-Layer De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Machine Learning (SL-ML) Engine (SL-XGBRanker). To prevent functional dilution from variants of uncertain significance, MBD4 loss-of-function (MBD4-LOF) was strictly restricted to truncating and canonical splice-site alleles (21 of 36 mutated lines), independently validated by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD; two-sided p2s = 0.0367), while excluding 15 lines harboring 19 non-truncating variants (18 missense, 1 inframe deletion). All primary pharmacogenomic comparisons were evaluated using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p2s), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity correction across six pre-specified candidate axes, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for expression equivalence. Results: Our analysis delineates three distinct therapeutic axes in MBD4-LOF tumors: (1) Cytidine Analog Vulnerability (Axis 1): Mechanistic structural evidence demonstrates that MBD4 loss impairs excision of 5-substituted pyrimidine analogs and deaminated bases, creating a direct biochemical bottleneck to gemcitabine and 5-fluorouracil incorporation. (2) ATR-Check1 Replication-Stress Vulnerability (Axis 2): In GDSC2 profiling, MBD4-LOF cell lines exhibit significant sensitivity to the ATR inhibitor ceralasertib (AZD6738). papers.title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects
papers.abstract: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.

papers.title: Deep learning-based enhancing spatial biological context parsing.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of spatial transcriptomics (ST) has established a foundation for the complementary integration of multimodal information from gene expression profiles, spatial localization, and histological images. However, noise and data heterogeneity complicate the characterization of spatial relationships and tissue structure. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework, CroSP, based on a multi-view graph autoencoder. The framework integrates gene expression profiles, spatial locations, and tissue morphology information into a low-dimensional latent representation. Cross-view contrastive learning and metric learning coordinate the complementary views. Across datasets from multiple platforms and spatial resolutions, CroSP improved spatial domain identification and delineated brain and olfactory bulb structures. Analyses using established downstream methods further characterized spatially variable genes and the spatial heterogeneity, immune microenvironments, and cell-cell communication in human breast cancer tissue. These results support the use of CroSP for spatial biological analysis in healthy and diseased tissues. Source code and tutorials: https://github.com/Biowust/CroSP.git. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22675113. Public raw datasets: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22533825.

papers.title: Impact of data quality on deep learning prediction of spatial transcriptomics from histology images.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomic technologies enable high-throughput quantification of gene expression at specific locations across tissue sections, facilitating insights into the spatial organization of biological processes. However, high costs associated with these technologies have motivated the development of deep learning methods to predict spatial gene expression from inexpensive hematoxylin and eosin-stained histology images. While most efforts have focused on modifying model architectures to boost predictive performance, the influence of training data quality remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate how variation in molecular and image data quality stemming from differences in spatial transcriptomic technologies impact deep learning-based gene expression prediction from histology images. To identify the aspects of data quality that impact predictive performance, we conduct in silico ablation experiments, which show that increased sparsity and noise in molecular data degrade predictive performance, while in silico rescue experiments via imputation provide only limited improvements that fail to generalize beyond the test set. Likewise, reduced image resolution can degrade predictive performance and further impacts model interpretability. We further demonstrate that these data quality-driven effects are reproducible across multiple spatial transcriptomics technologies and tissues, and remain consistent when using alternative feature extractors and model architectures. Overall, our results show how improving data quality provides an orthogonal strategy to tuning model architecture in spatial transcriptomics-based predictive modeling, highlighting the need to account for technology-specific limitations that directly impact data quality when developing predictive methodologies.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in multi-omics data integration: Advancing precision medicine, biomarker discovery and genomic-driven disease interventions
papers.abstract: The integration of multi-omics data—encompassing genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics—has revolutionized biomedical research, offering unprecedented insights into disease mechanisms and therapeutic interventions. However, the complexity and volume of multi-omics datasets present significant analytical challenges that traditional computational methods struggle to address. Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning and neural networks, has emerged as a powerful tool to overcome these limitations by enabling advanced data integration, biomarker discovery, and personalized treatment strategies. This paper explores the role of AI-driven multi-omics data integration in enhancing disease prediction, early diagnosis, and precision medicine. By leveraging AI models such as deep neural networks (DNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and transformers, researchers can analyze complex biological interactions, identify patterns indicative of disease onset, and stratify patient populations for tailored treatment approaches. Additionally, AI-powered feature selection methods facilitate the identification of disease-specific biomarkers across multiple omics layers, paving the way for more effective targeted therapies. Moreover, AI plays a crucial role in pharmacogenomics by predicting individualized drug responses, optimizing dosage regimens, and minimizing adverse drug reactions. Machine learning algorithms, including reinforcement learning and generative models, enable real-time modeling of drug-gene interactions, leading to safer and more efficacious therapeutic interventions. Despite the transformative potential of AI in multi-omics data analysis, challenges such as data standardization, model interpretability, and ethical considerations must be addressed to ensure reliability and clinical applicability. This paper provides a comprehensive review of AI-driven multi-omics research, highlighting current advancements, challenges, and future directions in precision medicine.
papers.venue: International Journal of Science and Research Archive

papers.title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

papers.title: Multiscale multimodal integration of spatial omics through a deep generative model with CORAL.
papers.abstract: Spatial omics enable the in situ characterization of tissue architecture by measuring molecular modalities. However, integrating these datasets remains challenging due to differences in spatial resolution, cross-modal alignment and molecular coverage. Here we show that Cross-scale spatial Omics Registration and Analysis via graph Learning (CORAL), a probabilistic deep generative model, leverages graph attention to integrate diverse spatial transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and epigenomic data across spatial scales. CORAL jointly models high-resolution datasets with limited molecular coverage and low-resolution genome-wide datasets, generating unified representations with broad molecular coverage and high spatial resolution. Across synthetic and experimental datasets from diverse tissues and platforms, CORAL accurately identifies spatial domains, predicts high-resolution molecular profiles, detects spatially variable genes and infers cell-cell interactions. Applied to spatial transcriptomic and proteomic data from hepatocellular carcinoma patients before and after immunotherapy, CORAL identified organized immune-cell subsets and signaling pathways associated with therapeutic resistance. These results demonstrate CORAL's broad applicability for resolving tissue organization and clinically relevant multicellular interactions.

papers.title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

papers.title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
papers.abstract: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.

papers.title: HINN prioritizes multi-omics biomarkers associated with cognitive decline.
papers.abstract: Integrating multi-omics data for disease prediction remains challenging due to the complexity of cross-layer biological interactions and the limited use of prior biological knowledge in many machine learning models. We present the Hierarchical Input Neural Network (HINN), a deep learning framework that incorporates biologically informed connections across genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic layers to model regulatory relationships in a structured and interpretable manner. HINN was applied to blood-derived multi-omics data to predict cognitive assessment scores, including Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 11 tasks (ADAS11), and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. A biologically guided feature construction pipeline was used to integrate genome-wide association studies-derived single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), promoter-region DNA methylation, and gene expression data through Gene Ontology Biological Process and KEGG pathway mappings. The model was evaluated using a rigorous training strategy that separates feature selection from testing and incorporates cross-validation as well as repeated runs to ensure robustness. Across all cognitive outcomes, HINN achieved the lowest mean normalized mean squared error among the evaluated models, with statistically significant improvements over most baseline methods. Ablation analyses showed that the contributions of individual omics modalities and biologically informed connectivity varied across cognitive outcomes, with the clearest benefits of structured connectivity observed for ADAS11 and MMSE. Feature attribution analysis identified a multi-omics cascade involving SNP (rs116557230), CpG site (cg24041822), and a SOCS4 gene expression probe, which showed consistent associations with multiple cognitive outcomes. These findings highlight the ability of HINN to uncover biologically meaningful cross-omics relationships relevant to cognitive decline. Together, this work demonstrates that integrating deep learning with biological knowledge enables biomarker discovery for complex diseases. All code, sample data, and instructions are publicly available via GitHub (https://github.com/bozdaglab/HINN) and archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19197057) to ensure reproducibility and long-term accessibility.

papers.title: ProFormer: generalizable classification of single-cell and plasma proteomes using deep learning.
papers.abstract: Proteins are the main drivers of cell function and disease, making proteomics a powerful technique for biomarker discovery and defining cell identity. While current technologies can profile thousands of proteins and reach single-cell sensitivity, limited throughput restricts applications such as robust classification of large biological or clinical cohorts. To close this gap, we present a deep-learning (DL) approach for the direct analysis of mass spectrometric (MS) data, assigning proteomic profiles to sample identity. Specifically, we introduce the ProFormer, a transformer pipeline that classifies samples by tabular MS1-level features derived from peptide ions, eliminating the need for time-consuming data interpretation. The ProFormer outperforms traditional machine-learning and image-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs), demonstrating enhanced classification and generalization over 14 evaluated architectures. We further provide detailed insights into how the ProFormer dynamically aggregates MS1 data, while preserving signal contribution and enabling explainable AI at single-peptide resolution. Applied to diverse LC-MS data sets, the ProFormer accurately classified single-cell proteomes by cell type, cycle stage or differentiation trajectory, as well as patient disease status from plasma proteomes. Thereby, the ProFormer provides a versatile and rapid framework for the classification of proteomic data, with important implications for patient stratification, early detection and single-cell analysis.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics prediction from histology jointly through Transformer and graph neural networks
papers.abstract: The rapid development of spatial transcriptomics allows the measurement of RNA abundance at a high spatial resolution, making it possible to simultaneously profile gene expression, spatial locations of cells or spots, and the corresponding hematoxylin and eosin-stained histology images. It turns promising to predict gene expression from histology images that are relatively easy and cheap to obtain. For this purpose, several methods are devised, but they have not fully captured the internal relations of the 2D vision features or spatial dependency between spots. Here, we developed Hist2ST, a deep learning-based model to predict RNA-seq expression from histology images. Around each sequenced spot, the corresponding histology image is cropped into an image patch and fed into a convolutional module to extract 2D vision features. Meanwhile, the spatial relations with the whole image and neighbored patches are captured through Transformer and graph neural network modules, respectively. These learned features are then used to predict the gene expression by following the zero-inflated negative binomial distribution. To alleviate the impact by the small spatial transcriptomics data, a self-distillation mechanism is employed for efficient learning of the model. By comprehensive tests on cancer and normal datasets, Hist2ST was shown to outperform existing methods in terms of both gene expression prediction and spatial region identification. Further pathway analyses indicated that our model could reserve biological information. Thus, Hist2ST enables generating spatial transcriptomics data from histology images for elucidating molecular signatures of tissues.

papers.title: Re-timing mortality risk through individualized modelling of lifespan trajectories.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk.

papers.title: Benchmarking DNA Foundation Models: Biological Blind Spots in Evo2 Variant-Effect Prediction
papers.abstract: DNA foundation models such as Evo2 and DNABERT-2 show promise for variant-effect prediction (VEP), yet rigorous benchmarks assessing their ability to capture established biological constraints remain limited. Here, we introduce controlled benchmarks based on well-characterized nuclear and mitochondrial sequence features. Although Evo2 achieves strong aggregate performance on mitochondrial variants (AUROC = 0.927), our analyses reveal systematic blind spots in short-range signals, including codon usage bias, as well as spurious sensitivity to biologically neutral sequence context. Notably, changes in flanking sequences can cause pathogenic tRNA variants to be misclassified as benign. These findings suggest that Evo2's predictive performance may rely more heavily on learned sequence regularities than on the biological constraints governing variant function, raising concerns about the clinical utility of zero-shot genomic foundation models.Our framework provides a principled basis for standardized model evaluation and for guiding the development of architectures better aligned with biological constraints.

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
papers.abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children's Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

papers.title: scTransMIL bridges patient-level disease states and single-cell transcriptomics for cancer screening and heterogeneity inference.
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing offers profound insights into tumor complexity. However, reliably linking individual cellular profiles to overall sample-level phenotypes remains computationally challenging, particularly when cell-specific annotations are absent. This disconnect limits the technology's utility in studying underlying tumor mechanisms. Here we show how scTransMIL, an artificial intelligence framework, bridges this gap. By conceptualizing a biological sample as a collection of individual cells, scTransMIL employs a transformer-based multi-instance learning approach to directly connect single-cell transcriptomic profiles with overarching sample-level labels. We demonstrate that scTransMIL accurately predicts sample-level cancer phenotypes, including the tissue-of-origin for metastatic tumors. At cellular resolution, it robustly identifies tumor-associated cell populations and maps biological progression trajectories using only minimal sample-level annotations. Furthermore, the model's attention mechanisms facilitate full-transcriptome biomarker discovery. By systematically integrating molecular and cellular scales with broader phenotypic states, our approach provides a computational tool to dissect tumor heterogeneity and advance fundamental cancer biology.

papers.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
papers.abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

papers.title: Graph-guided flow matching enables biologically informed prediction at single-cell resolution
papers.abstract: Perturb-seq enables systematic interrogation of massively parallel genetic perturbations at single-cell resolution, yet exhaustive characterization of the full perturbation space remains impractical. Here, we present Graph-guided Flow Matching (GFM), a generative framework that integrates biological knowledge graphs with latent flow matching to predict post-perturbation single-cell transcriptomes. Across multiple large-scale Perturb-seq datasets, GFM outperforms a strong linear baseline and current deep-learning models in predicting unseen single-gene perturbations, while training up to 30x faster and remaining robust with limited training data. GFM also demonstrates competitive performance in the two-gene perturbation prediction task when neither perturbed gene is observed during training. Ablation experiments show that combining flow matching with knowledge graphs enables accurate prediction of perturbation responses. Finally, GFM accurately calculates transcriptional consequences of HSP90AA1 inactivation and identifies target candidates unseen by the model in chronic myeloid leukemia. Our study establishes GFM as a biologically informed generative framework that predicts single-cell perturbation responses for prioritization of therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

papers.title: Predicting transcriptional interactions with GrnPFN
papers.abstract: Combinatorial therapies offer opportunities to improve treatment efficacy and overcome therapeutic resistance, but their rational design requires understanding how combined interventions interact beyond their individual effects. Combined genetic and chemical perturbations can elicit nonadditive transcriptional responses, yet the vast number of possible combinations limits experimental characterization. Predicting these interactions is particularly challenging when few or no combinations have been measured. Here we present GrnPFN, a prior-data fitted network that predicts nonadditive transcriptional responses to combinations from single-perturbation profiles. Pretrained on simulated screens generated from random gene-regulatory networks, GrnPFN incorporates measured combinations through in-context learning without retraining. We evaluated GrnPFN in single-cell screens spanning CRISPR activation, RNA knockdown and drug combinations, using separate cells to construct model inputs, training targets and test targets. Without measured combinations in the target screen, GrnPFN outperformed gradient boosting trained on other screens. With limited combination measurements, it outperformed kernel ridge regression fitted to the same measured pairs. These advantages extended to an additional screen combining CRISPR interference with a drug. Our results demonstrate that pretraining on simulated regulatory networks enables prediction of nonadditive transcriptional interactions across perturbation modalities when experimental measurements are scarce.

papers.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

papers.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
papers.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

papers.title: Real-world deployment of a fine-tuned pathology foundation model for lung cancer biomarker detection
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence models using digital histopathology slides stained with hematoxylin and eosin offer promising, tissue-preserving diagnostic tools for patients with cancer. Despite their advantages, their clinical utility in real-world settings remains unproven. Assessing EGFR mutations in lung adenocarcinoma demands rapid, accurate and cost-effective tests that preserve tissue for genomic sequencing. PCR-based assays provide rapid results but with reduced accuracy compared with next-generation sequencing and require additional tissue. Computational biomarkers leveraging modern foundation models can address these limitations. Here we assembled a large international clinical dataset of digital lung adenocarcinoma slides (N = 8,461) to develop a computational EGFR biomarker. Our model fine-tunes an open-source foundation model, improving task-specific performance with out-of-center generalization and clinical-grade accuracy on primary and metastatic specimens (mean area under the curve: internal 0.847, external 0.870). To evaluate real-world clinical translation, we conducted a prospective silent trial of the biomarker on primary samples, achieving an area under the curve of 0.890. The artificial-intelligence-assisted workflow reduced the number of rapid molecular tests needed by up to 43% while maintaining the current clinical standard performance. Our retrospective and prospective analyses demonstrate the real-world clinical utility of a computational pathology biomarker.

papers.title: SpaAxFormer: Fine-Grained Token Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics with Axial Transformers
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics combines gene-expression measurements with spatial relationships between cells. We investigate how spatial context can be incorporated into gene-resolved representations while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence. SpaAxFormer is a spatially constrained factorized formulation that maintains contextual cell-gene states throughout the encoder. It first contextualizes genes within each cell and then exchanges corresponding gene states across spatial neighbors, while a separate CLS representation provides a cell-level summary. Contextual gene states support gene-expression reconstruction, while CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive learning provide complementary supervision for the cell-level representation. We evaluate SpaAxFormer on gene-expression imputation and spatial-domain identification across multiple spatial-transcriptomics technologies. Compared with the included baselines, imputation results were most favorable on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) datasets and more mixed on additional technologies, while post-hoc spatial refinement consistently improved mean ARI on the Visium spatial-domain datasets where it was applied. In a single-slice component-addition analysis, mean clustering ARI increased as CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive supervision were added. Together, these results show that the same gene-resolved formulation can support complementary gene-level prediction and cell-level spatial representation while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence.

papers.title: Vermeer: Autoregressive generative modeling of microscopy predicts protein localization
papers.abstract: Fluorescent microscopy provides a rich view into how proteins localize within cells, but it remains experimentally infeasible to image human proteins across all of the different factors that can impact localization. We introduce Vermeer, a channel-adaptive autoregressive generative model for in silico generation of microscopy images of protein localization. Vermeer conditions generations on protein sequences and landmark stains showing the morphology of cells, which enables it to generalize to unseen proteins and cell lines. We show that Vermeer, trained on the Human Protein Atlas, can generate images with substantially improved perceptual quality and biological fidelity over previous proposals. Additionally, Vermeer's autoregressive framework enables flexible generation using varying channel subsets and orderings, enabling zero-shot transfer to data collected under different imaging conditions and channel configurations than those used for training. These results position Vermeer to enable scalable modeling of protein localization and is a step towards generative foundation models that can operate over distinct microscopy datasets. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/vermeer.git.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: Multi-omics profiling links epigenetic and lncRNA changes to early human endochondral ossification priming
papers.abstract: Differentiation programs remain incompletely understood across stem cell types, including for human bone marrow mesenchymal stromal/stem (BM-MSCs) cells, a heterogenous population orchestrating bone formation and establishing a functional hematopoietic niche in the bone marrow. BM-MSCs form and repair bone through the evolutionarily conserved process of endochondral ossification (EO), initiated by deposition of a transient cartilage template subsequently remodeled into bone and bone marrow tissues. Despite their considerable potential for skeletal regeneration, the early molecular and cellular events underlying BM-MSCs commitment to EO remain elusive. To overcome donor dependent variability in chondrogenic potential that limits mechanistic studies, we here exploit OssiGel as a potent chondro-inductive extracellular matrix offering robust recapitulation of EO by BMMSCs. Through multi-omics profiling of OssiGel-primed BM-MSCs, we identify rapid chromatin remodeling at chondrogenic loci as concomitant for lineage commitment. The emergence of a chondro-progenitor population is detected as early as 3 days in vivo and correlates with successful EO recapitulation. Mechanistically, we identify LINC02511 as novel enhancer-associated element involved in the onset of EO. We confirm presence of LINC02511 in human skeletal atlases, and its CRISPR-mediated silencing significantly impaired EO. By integrating human tissue engineering strategies with single cell multi-omics profiling, our study provides a framework for deciphering BM-MSCs fate decisions, highlighting the role of enhancer and non-coding elements as key determinants of early lineage specification. These findings advance our understanding of BM-MSCs biology and will prompt their translational exploitation in regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Spatially informed clustering, integration, and deconvolution of spatial transcriptomics with GraphST
papers.abstract: Abstract Advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies have enabled the gene expression profiling of tissues while retaining its spatial context. Effective exploitation of this data combination requires spatially informed analysis tools to perform three key tasks, spatial clustering, multi-sample integration, and cell type deconvolution. Here, we present GraphST, a novel graph self-supervised contrastive learning method that incorporates spatial location information and gene expression profiles to accomplish all three tasks in a streamlined process while outperforming existing methods in each task. GraphST combines graph neural networks with self-supervised contrastive learning to learn informative and discriminative spot representations by minimizing the embedding distance between spatially adjacent spots and vice versa. With GraphST, we achieved 10% higher clustering accuracy on multiple datasets than competing methods, and better delineated the fine-grained structures in tissues such as the brain and embryo. Moreover, GraphST is the only method that can jointly analyze multiple tissue slices in both vertical and horizontal integration while correcting for batch effects. Lastly, compared to other methods, GraphST’s cell type deconvolution achieved higher accuracy on simulated data and better captured spatial niches such as the germinal centers of the lymph node in experimentally acquired data. We further showed that GraphST can recover the immune cell distribution in different regions of breast tumor tissue and reveal spatial niches with exhausted tumor infiltrating T cells. Through our examples, we demonstrated that GraphST is widely applicable to a broad range of tissue types and technology platforms. In summary, GraphST is a streamlined, user friendly and computationally efficient tool for characterizing tissue complexity and gaining biological insights into the spatial organization within tissues.

papers.title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

papers.title: PlantPAN 5.0: updated database for integrating multiomics evidence and exploring multilayered transcriptional regulatory networks in plants.
papers.abstract: Plant Promoter Analysis Navigator (PlantPAN) 5.0 (https://plantpan.itps.ncku.edu.tw/) is an integrated multiomics resource for investigating plant cis-regulatory elements and transcriptional regulatory networks. This release expands genome annotations and promoter sequences to 240 species and provides 71 040 transcription factor (TF) annotations and 7762 nonredundant binding matrices. Its companion database, PCBase 3.0, substantially expands ChIP-seq data and newly incorporates ATAC-seq, bisulfite-sequencing, and four Hi-C-based chromatin interaction datasets for Arabidopsis thaliana. The new Differential Analysis function enables comparison of TF binding, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation across conditions. The redesigned Promoter Analysis interface provides TF family-level statistics, with a Pattern Overview panel integrating TF-binding site (TFBS) densities, plant DNA large language model-predicted open-chromatin regions, CpG-rich regions, and tandem repeats. Two new modules are introduced: (i) Transcriptome Regulatory Analysis and Coexpression, where candidate regulatory TFs and shared cis-elements in gene sets are prioritized through differential expression and coexpression analysis, and (ii) Interaction Topology Analysis for Chromatin and TFs, where chromatin interaction regions are integrated to reveal potentially coregulated genes and their shared TFs and predicted TFBSs. A Dockerized package enables large-scale local promoter analyses, with data privacy. Therefore, PlantPAN 5.0 is a comprehensive framework for discovering plant transcriptional regulatory mechanisms.

papers.title: Environment-Aware DNA Language Model for Stress-Responsive Genomic Prioritization in Maize
papers.abstract: Abiotic stresses such as heat and drought severely reduce the productivity of major crops including maize, with adverse implications for agricultural sustainability. Despite progress in characterizing stress resilience, identifying genomic regions associated with stress response remains challenging due to complex genotype-by-environment interactions. Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs), inspired by advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), leverage large-scale self-supervised pre-training on DNA sequences to capture regulatory patterns; however, their adaptation to plant stress-response analysis remains underexplored. In this work, we propose an environment-aware DNA-LLM framework that incorporates stress-specific prompt tokens into AgroNT, a transformer-based plant GFM, using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). The model learns stress-conditioned genomic representations that exhibit distinct structures across environmental contexts. We further formulate a prioritization method that uses stress-induced shifts in these representations relative to the control condition together with stress-token-associated transformer attention patterns to identify putative stress-responsive genomic regions. The framework was evaluated on the Genomes-to-Fields (G2F) dataset, comprising over 4,000 maize hybrids grown across 38 locations over 8 years, using grain yield under heat, drought, and combined heat-drought stress. Flowering traits were used to assess generalizability of the stress-conditioned representations across phenotypes. The prioritized regions were assessed using spatiotemporal differential gene-expression profiles, stress-associated quantitative trait loci, and transcription-factor characterization. Regulatory motif analysis further revealed stress-associated motifs enriched within the prioritized sequences as well as model-emphasized high-attention regions. Functional annotation of genes proximal to prioritized regions highlighted roles in transcriptional regulation, signaling, and metabolic pathways relevant to abiotic stress adaptation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the potential of stress-conditioned transformer-based sequence modeling for environment-aware genome-to-phenome analysis in crop improvement.

papers.title: Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.

papers.title: Conditional diffusion for single-cell Hi-C data imputation and enhancement with scHiC-Diff.
papers.abstract: Single-cell high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (scHi-C) enables the analysis of cell-to-cell variability in three-dimensional (3D) genome organization, but its utility is severely limited by pervasive technical dropouts, leading to extremely sparse contact maps. Accurately identifying dropout events and imputing the corresponding missing chromatin contacts remains a challenging problem, as technical dropouts are confounded with genuine absences of chromatin interactions. Existing imputation and enhancement methods often rely on smoothing strategies or restrictive parametric likelihood assumptions, which may obscure fine-scale chromatin structures and cell-specific features. Here, we present scHiC-Diff, a conditional diffusion-based framework for scHi-C data imputation and enhancement. scHiC-Diff employs a forward process that progressively perturbs contact maps and a reverse denoising process that reconstructs chromatin interactions from noisy observations. To better capture long-range dependencies in complex 3D genome structures, scHi-C contact matrices are treated as masked images and modeled using a Diffusion Transformer (DiT). Across two complementary simulated datasets and three real scHi-C datasets, scHiC-Diff improves the recovery of chromatin interaction patterns and enhances downstream analyses compared with existing methods. Application to a developmental scHi-C dataset further demonstrates improved reconstruction of chromatin organization and enhanced chromatin loop detection.

papers.title: scPolyA enables efficient, interactive and agent-guided alternative polyadenylation analysis in single-cell and spatial transcriptomes
papers.abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) changes which regulatory sequences an RNA retains, creating a layer of cellular variation that gene-level expression profiles cannot resolve. Here we present scPolyA, a unified, AI-enabled framework that transforms conventional single-cell and spatial 3'-end transcriptomes into quantitative maps of RNA-end choice. scPolyA connects de novo poly(A)-site discovery to cell- and spot-resolved measurements of terminal-site usage, 3' untranslated region length and intronic polyadenylation, enabling differential APA analysis across cell states and tissue regions. Its integrated deep-learning module, DeepCPS, improves recognition of sparsely supported poly(A) sites and predicts cleavage positions at nucleotide resolution. An integrated graphical workspace brings parameter exploration, efficient rerunning and genome browsing together, while an APA-specialised AI agent translates natural-language research questions into executed analyses, verified outputs and evidence-guided interpretation. Across diverse single-cell protocols and spatial platforms, scPolyA achieves higher reference-atlas agreement than most evaluated de novo methods, while single-cell benchmarks demonstrate competitive runtime and memory use. Applied to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, scPolyA reveals recurrent 3' untranslated region shortening in tumour keratinocytes across all ten patients and corresponding patterns in tumour-enriched regions, with tissue-level contrasts shaped by cellular composition. scPolyA extends conventional transcriptomics from gene abundance to RNA-end regulation, linking transcript choices to cellular states and tissue organisation.

papers.title: Building from the ground up: augmentation strategies to improve protein language model performance on protein sets
papers.abstract: An important underlying requirement for deep learning models is the availability of large datasets, however, in sciences such as chemistry and biology, generating experimental data of sufficient size represents a significant bottleneck. In this work, we probed the extent and nature of limited input data, characterize how several protein language models (pLMs) learned on suboptimal datasets, and investigated augmentation approaches to improve predictive model performance. We found that narrowing the distribution of protein-protein complexes in a limited dataset permits an order-of-magnitude decrease in training dataset size, if a model is only expected to generalize to in-distribution data. Similar results were found in active learning (AL), where both in- and out-of-distribution Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) showed a small but consistent increase upon augmentation of the training set with complexes produced by ESM-3, a generative pLM.

papers.title: Conditional out-of-distribution generation for unpaired data using transfer VAE
papers.abstract: MOTIVATION: While generative models have shown great success in sampling high-dimensional samples conditional on low-dimensional descriptors (stroke thickness in MNIST, hair color in CelebA, speaker identity in WaveNet), their generation out-of-distribution poses fundamental problems due to the difficulty of learning compact joint distribution across conditions. The canonical example of the conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE), for instance, does not explicitly relate conditions during training and, hence, has no explicit incentive of learning such a compact representation. RESULTS: We overcome the limitation of the CVAE by matching distributions across conditions using maximum mean discrepancy in the decoder layer that follows the bottleneck. This introduces a strong regularization both for reconstructing samples within the same condition and for transforming samples across conditions, resulting in much improved generalization. As this amount to solving a style-transfer problem, we refer to the model as transfer VAE (trVAE). Benchmarking trVAE on high-dimensional image and single-cell RNA-seq, we demonstrate higher robustness and higher accuracy than existing approaches. We also show qualitatively improved predictions by tackling previously problematic minority classes and multiple conditions in the context of cellular perturbation response to treatment and disease based on high-dimensional single-cell gene expression data. For generic tasks, we improve Pearson correlations of high-dimensional estimated means and variances with their ground truths from 0.89 to 0.97 and 0.75 to 0.87, respectively. We further demonstrate that trVAE learns cell-type-specific responses after perturbation and improves the prediction of most cell-type-specific genes by 65%. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The trVAE implementation is available via github.com/theislab/trvae. The results of this article can be reproduced via github.com/theislab/trvae_reproducibility.

papers.title: GenSLMs: Genome-scale language models reveal SARS-CoV-2 evolutionary dynamics
papers.abstract: We seek to transform how new and emergent variants of pandemic-causing viruses, specifically SARS-CoV-2, are identified and classified. By adapting large language models (LLMs) for genomic data, we build genome-scale language models (GenSLMs) which can learn the evolutionary landscape of SARS-CoV-2 genomes. By pre-training on over 110 million prokaryotic gene sequences and fine-tuning a SARS-CoV-2-specific model on 1.5 million genomes, we show that GenSLMs can accurately and rapidly identify variants of concern. Thus, to our knowledge, GenSLMs represents one of the first whole genome scale foundation models which can generalize to other prediction tasks. We demonstrate scaling of GenSLMs on GPU-based supercomputers and AI-hardware accelerators utilizing 1.63 Zettaflops in training runs with a sustained performance of 121 PFLOPS in mixed precision and peak of 850 PFLOPS. We present initial scientific insights from examining GenSLMs in tracking evolutionary dynamics of SARS-CoV-2, paving the path to realizing this on large biological data.
papers.venue: The International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications

papers.title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise.
papers.abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

papers.title: ProteinBERT: a universal deep-learning model of protein sequence and function
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: Self-supervised deep language modeling has shown unprecedented success across natural language tasks, and has recently been repurposed to biological sequences. However, existing models and pretraining methods are designed and optimized for text analysis. We introduce ProteinBERT, a deep language model specifically designed for proteins. Our pretraining scheme combines language modeling with a novel task of Gene Ontology (GO) annotation prediction. We introduce novel architectural elements that make the model highly efficient and flexible to long sequences. The architecture of ProteinBERT consists of both local and global representations, allowing end-to-end processing of these types of inputs and outputs. ProteinBERT obtains near state-of-the-art performance, and sometimes exceeds it, on multiple benchmarks covering diverse protein properties (including protein structure, post-translational modifications and biophysical attributes), despite using a far smaller and faster model than competing deep-learning methods. Overall, ProteinBERT provides an efficient framework for rapidly training protein predictors, even with limited labeled data. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/nadavbra/protein_bert. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics.
papers.abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

papers.title: Biobank-scale self-supervised genotype pretraining yields transferable representations for human genetics.
papers.abstract: Biobank-scale genotyping has created unprecedented cohorts for human genetics, yet the field still lacks scalable methods for learning transferable representations from largely unlabeled individual-level genotype data. Here, we introduce SNPBERT, a self-supervised transformer pretrained on genotypes from 485 923 UK Biobank participants using masked rsID prediction. SNPBERT embeddings recovered known population structure across UK Biobank and three external datasets, performed comparably to principal component analysis, and supported the identification of ancestry-informative marker SNPs. Fine-tuning with an attention-based multiple-instance head generated disease-specific risk scores that provided complementary information beyond conventional polygenic risk scores.
