The corresponding two-layer comparison shows little additional benefit from non-human PPI edges, consistent with the greater message-passing depth needed to transmit their information. For human proteins excluded from training interactions, multispecies HGT achieves $0.8335\pm0.0094$ AP versus $0.6482\pm0.0052$ for a sequence-only pair model. These results identify the value, depth dependence, and limits of evolutionary graph context while distinguishing prediction of held-out edges from generalization to held-out proteins.

papers.title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

papers.title: Beyond Discrete Ancestry Groups: Distribution-Aware In-Context Learning for Cancer Outcome Prediction Across the Genetic Ancestry Continuum
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for omics-based prediction of cancer outcomes are commonly built on aggregated data without distinguishing ancestry groups, or under an ancestry-discrete design, which partitions samples into ancestry groups and fits a separate model within each group. Recent evidence shows that this approach is inherently limited: predictive accuracy declines with genetic distance from the training samples, even within a single ancestry group, because the data distribution shifts continuously rather than only between predefined categories. In this paper, we propose distribution-aware in-context learning (DA-ICL) for ancestry-continuum modeling. Our method extends conventional ancestry-discrete modeling to ancestry-continuum modeling, capturing the nonstationary omics-endpoint relationship across the genetic continuum while enabling efficient modeling through an in-context learning foundation model. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating the superiority of the ancestry-continuum over ancestry-discrete modeling, along with empirical results supporting the proposed framework. Source code is available at https://github.com/ai4pm/DA-ICL-Continuum.

papers.title: Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency
papers.abstract: Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. We propose FlowAlign, a flow-guided target-space alignment method that repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model. FlowAlign uses the learned flow field to guide the alignment of source-side representations with the fixed target space, encouraging them to preserve paired correspondence while remaining compatible with the global target-space structure. We further provide theoretical analysis showing how FlowAlign helps improve paired correspondence by controlling endpoint accuracy and capturing local target-space geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image--text alignment demonstrate that FlowAlign improves instance level correspondence while preserving target-space structure across different modality settings.

papers.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

papers.title: Predicting dynamic expression patterns in budding yeast with a fungal DNA language model
papers.abstract: Predicting gene expression from DNA sequence remains challenging due to complex regulatory codes. We introduce a masked DNA language model pretrained on 165 fungal genomes related to budding yeast that learns conserved regulatory sequence motifs. Fine-tuning the LM on yeast RNA-seq data--including high-resolution transcriptional regulator induction time courses generated in this study--yielded Shorkie, a model that substantially improves gene expression prediction compared to baselines trained without self-supervision. Shorkie identified canonical transcription factor (TF) binding motifs and captured changes in their regulatory contributions across induction time courses. Furthermore, Shorkie accurately predicted variant effects, outperforming leading sequence-to-expression models in cis-eQTL classification and achieving high concordance with massively parallel reporter assays. Interpretability analyses revealed Shorkie's ability to resolve promoter dynamics, splicing signals, and temporal changes in regulatory motif usage. Together, these results support combining pretraining on related fungal genomes with RNA-seq fine-tuning to improve sequence-based prediction of gene expression in budding yeast and provide insights into noncoding variants.

papers.title: A Dynamic Stem Cell State Links Environmental Cues to Skeletal and Regenerative Fates
papers.abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.

papers.title: Learning Strand-Equivariant Tokenizations of DNA with MirrorDNA
papers.abstract: DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer. Yet DNA language models are tokenized, trained and tested on one strand at a time. We show that this makes them inconsistent. BPE and $k$-mer tokenizers split 92--100\% of transcription-factor motifs differently on the two strands, and NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA change 25-31\% of their predictions when the test sequences are reverse-complemented. We introduce {\model}, a compact DNA language model with a learned tokenizer that guarantees mirror-symmetric token boundaries across reverse-complement sequences, regardless of its learned parameters. We prove that this symmetry holds through the whole model. As a result, the same model can give identical answers on both strands when the label does not depend on the strand, and can still tell the strands apart when it does, which no strand-blind model can learn. Counting only predictions that are correct on both strands, \model\ more than doubles the MCC of NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA. With 2.3M parameters, it is more accurate than the Caduceus models trained on the same data, and not significantly different from NT-v2 (98M parameters) on Genomic Benchmarks or from DNABERT-2 (117M) on the Nucleotide Transformer tasks. It also stays accurate on inputs sixteen times longer than those it was trained on. The same model trained with reverse-complement augmentation instead still changes about one prediction in ten with the strand, unless its outputs are averaged over both strands. Without any annotation, the tokenizer learns to keep the splice-donor signal \texttt{AGGT} in a single token. Code: https://github.com/NIRJHOR-DATTA/MirrorDNA.

papers.title: Multimodal data-driven clustering analysis of heart failure patients identifies two distinct patterns of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: Results from the PACIFIC-PRESERVED study.
papers.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for over half of heart failure cases but remains poorly defined due to its clinical heterogeneity. In the prospective PACIFIC-Preserved cohort (NCT04189029, n = 155), we applied multimodal deep phenotyping, including high-throughput proteomics, and unsupervised machine learning to identify biologically distinct HFpEF subgroups. Multiview clustering revealed two major HFpEF phenogroups: PEF1, characterized by inflammatory signaling, TNF receptor activation, cardio-skeletal injury, and greater renal dysfunction; and PEF2, marked by endothelial stress and milder perturbations. Conventional diagnostics alone could not reliably distinguish these subgroups, but a multimodal classifier integrating clinical, imaging, and proteomic variables achieved high predictive accuracy (F1-score 0.87). External validation in the MEDIA-DHF cohort (n = 456) confirmed that PEF1 was independently associated with adverse outcomes (adjusted HR 2.27, 95% CI 1.04-4.94). These findings establish a classifier-driven, biologically informed stratification of HFpEF, providing a framework for precision medicine in heart failure.

papers.title: Protein large language model-assisted one-to-one gene homology mapping in cross-species single-cell transcriptome integration.
papers.abstract: Cross-species integration of single-cell transcriptomes requires establishing gene correspondences to enable comparative analysis of expression profiles across organisms. Current approaches predominantly rely on Ensembl homology tables; although gene-family expansion and contraction can reflect biologically meaningful evolutionary divergence, default many-to-many mappings can overweight expanded gene-family signals during integration and generate mapping-associated microclusters that lack clear cell-type identity, thereby complicating direct cell-type alignment. Although restricting mappings to a one-to-one scheme suppresses such artifacts, it reduces the number of homology gene pairs by ∼8% (about 900 pairs). To address this limitation, we develop a protein large language model (pLLM)-based gene homology mapping strategy that boosts the number of homology gene pairs. By enforcing a one-to-one mapping constraint and integrating pLLM-derived representations with sequence similarity, we construct a fused mapping approach, which achieves top performance in a comprehensive benchmark based on a curated cross-species atlas spanning nine data sets, 11 species, and more than 3.2 million cells. Our method further identifies previously unannotated cell-type marker pairs, facilitating novel cross-species marker discovery. These results establish a robust framework for gene homology mapping in cross-species transcriptome integration, improving both accuracy and biological interpretability.

papers.title: CytoVI: deep generative modeling of antibody-based single cell data.
papers.abstract: Antibody-based single-cell technologies, such as flow cytometry, mass cytometry and CITE-seq, have become widely used in clinical diagnostics and basic research; however, their analysis is complicated by technical noise, batch effects, platform differences and restricted antibody panels. Here we present CytoVI, a probabilistic generative model for statistically rigorous unified analysis of antibody-based single-cell data. CytoVI generates informative cell embeddings, imputes missing measurements, performs differential protein expression testing and automates annotation of cells in a single probabilistic model. We applied CytoVI to build an integrated B cell maturation atlas spanning 350 proteins and identified proteins associated with immunoglobulin class-switching. In a cohort of patients with B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma profiled by flow cytometry and CITE-seq, CytoVI uncovered disease-associated T cell states. CytoVI is available as open-source software at scvi-tools.org .

papers.title: Function-preserving watermarking of AI-generated proteins.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) models are revolutionizing biology, with tools such as AlphaFold 3 and protein design models accelerating breakthroughs in protein structure prediction and the creation of new functional proteins1. Tracking and establishing the provenance of AI-generated protein sequences and structures is becoming increasingly important to tackle a range of emerging challenges, including biosecurity and concerns about information veracity2-4. Here we introduce SynthIDBio, a family of methods for watermarking protein sequences and structures to establish the provenance of those generated with AI. SynthIDBio-sequence actively embeds a watermark into protein sequences while preserving function. We demonstrate this by creating watermarked, functional designed protein binders with binding affinity comparable with non-watermarked counterparts and near-perfect watermark detection accuracy. Furthermore, SynthIDBio-structure, a fine-tuned AlphaFold3 model, embeds an imperceptible watermark into biomolecular structures. Our work is a proof-of-concept that function-preserving biological watermarking is feasible, introducing a potential tool for provenance in the rapidly expanding era of AI-driven biological engineering.

papers.title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
papers.abstract: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

papers.title: TACFormer: Transformer-Based Generative Model for Target-Conditioned De Novo PROTAC Design
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents a fundamental shift in drug discovery, moving beyond traditional target inhibition toward the event-driven removal of disease-causing proteins. A prominent strategy for TPD is the use of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that selectively route a protein of interest (POI) to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation. While PROTAC design still relies heavily on trial-and-error synthesis and experimental testing, deep generative models offer a promising means to explore PROTAC chemical space in silico and generate novel molecules. However, many existing generative methods formulate PROTAC design primarily as a linker-generation problem, with POI-binding (warhead) and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance. This restricts exploration of the full PROTAC chemical space and often leaves the POI implicit through the predefined warhead, rather than using protein-level information as an explicit conditioning signal during generation. To address these limitations, we propose TACFormer: a transformer-based generative model for target-aware de novo PROTAC design. The model conditions a GPT-style molecular decoder on pretrained ESM-2 representations of POI sequences, allowing POI-level information to steer full-molecule generation. Our results show that TACFormer generates highly novel and chemically diverse PROTACs while showing consistent POI-dependent shifts in generated chemical space. In particular, molecules generated under specific target conditions preferentially populate chemical neighborhoods associated with POIs in the held-out dataset, while extrapolating to novel chemotypes. By natively integrating biological context into the generative process, TACFormer moves PROTAC design toward a more biology-informed exploration of degrader chemical space.

papers.title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
papers.abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

papers.title: HELIOS: A spatial omics-informed multi-organ cell atlas enables AI-based tumour microenvironment profiling and biomarker discovery from routine histopathology
papers.abstract: Spatial omics defines tumour microenvironments with high biological resolution but remains difficult to scale across large clinical cohorts. We developed HELIOS (H&E Learning Informed by Omics and Spatial Profiling), which transfers spatial-omics-derived cell identities into routine haematoxylin and eosin histology for interpretable single-cell tumour microenvironment profiling. HELIOS integrates 12.9 million cells from 60 specimens across 13 tissue types and four spatial profiling platforms, spanning eight epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular populations. The resulting multiclass detector generalised across independent histopathology benchmarks. Applied to colorectal, breast, and lung cancers, HELIOS recapitulated molecular subtype-associated microenvironment states and identified prognostic immune and stromal phenotypes. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes were consistently associated with favourable outcomes, whereas neutrophil and fibroblast phenotypes showed cancer-specific associations. HELIOS-derived features remained prognostic after adjustment for clinicopathological and molecular variables. These findings demonstrate that spatial omics can provide scalable biological supervision for extracting clinically relevant tumour microenvironment features from routine H&E, supporting scalable risk stratification and biomarker development across clinical cohorts and retrospective pathology archives.

papers.title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
papers.abstract: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.

papers.title: Image-based consensus molecular subtype (imCMS) classification of colorectal cancer using deep learning
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Complex phenotypes captured on histological slides represent the biological processes at play in individual cancers, but the link to underlying molecular classification has not been clarified or systematised. In colorectal cancer (CRC), histological grading is a poor predictor of disease progression, and consensus molecular subtypes (CMSs) cannot be distinguished without gene expression profiling. We hypothesise that image analysis is a cost-effective tool to associate complex features of tissue organisation with molecular and outcome data and to resolve unclassifiable or heterogeneous cases. In this study, we present an image-based approach to predict CRC CMS from standard H&E sections using deep learning. DESIGN: Training and evaluation of a neural network were performed using a total of n=1206 tissue sections with comprehensive multi-omic data from three independent datasets (training on FOCUS trial, n=278 patients; test on rectal cancer biopsies, GRAMPIAN cohort, n=144 patients; and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), n=430 patients). Ground truth CMS calls were ascertained by matching random forest and single sample predictions from CMS classifier. RESULTS: Image-based CMS (imCMS) accurately classified slides in unseen datasets from TCGA (n=431 slides, AUC)=0.84) and rectal cancer biopsies (n=265 slides, AUC=0.85). imCMS spatially resolved intratumoural heterogeneity and provided secondary calls correlating with bioinformatic prediction from molecular data. imCMS classified samples previously unclassifiable by RNA expression profiling, reproduced the expected correlations with genomic and epigenetic alterations and showed similar prognostic associations as transcriptomic CMS. CONCLUSION: This study shows that a prediction of RNA expression classifiers can be made from H&E images, opening the door to simple, cheap and reliable biological stratification within routine workflows.

papers.title: Nucleotide Transformer: building and evaluating robust foundation models for human genomics
papers.abstract: The prediction of molecular phenotypes from DNA sequences remains a longstanding challenge in genomics, often driven by limited annotated data and the inability to transfer learnings between tasks. Here, we present an extensive study of foundation models pre-trained on DNA sequences, named Nucleotide Transformer, ranging from 50 million up to 2.5 billion parameters and integrating information from 3,202 human genomes and 850 genomes from diverse species. These transformer models yield context-specific representations of nucleotide sequences, which allow for accurate predictions even in low-data settings. We show that the developed models can be fine-tuned at low cost to solve a variety of genomics applications. Despite no supervision, the models learned to focus attention on key genomic elements and can be used to improve the prioritization of genetic variants. The training and application of foundational models in genomics provides a widely applicable approach for accurate molecular phenotype prediction from DNA sequence. Nucleotide Transformer is a series of genomics foundation models of different parameter sizes and training datasets that can be applied to various downstream tasks by fine-tuning.

papers.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences it generates rather than treating the model as a black box. Candidate sequences were filtered based on predicted Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) along with human insights into the structural activities of the AMPs in bacterial membranes, and a final set of peptides was selected for experimental testing. Biological assays for determining MIC confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, with fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements providing structural insight. With our XSI approach, we are able to reveal correlations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties of these sequences to bacterial membrane mimics, that directly correlate with biological activities in cell-based assays. This builds confidence in that the learned amino acid interdependencies as applied to AMPs carries physico-chemical meaning and is relevant for discoveries of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can serve as effective and transparent tools for rational AMP discovery.

papers.title: Physiological mapping and prediction reveal stress-responsive translation initiation landscapes
papers.abstract: Translation initiation defines the protein output of the transcriptome, but its physiological dynamics in cells and tissues remain incompletely characterized. Here we develop TISCA2, an inhibitor-free method that captures eIF5B-associated initiating ribosomes to map translation initiation sites genome-wide. By directly identifying start sites rather than inferring translation from elongating-ribosome periodicity, TISCA2 improves the detection of short and overlapping translons. Translation of a subset of TISCA2-identified translons is supported by N-terminal proteomics and HLA-I immunopeptidomics. The arsenite-induced integrated stress response broadly redistributes start-site usage, reducing upstream initiation in favor of downstream initiation. TISCA2 further reveals tissue-specific initiation landscapes in vivo, with increased detection of downstream candidate start sites in the testis. Finally, we develop IncepTIS, a sequence-based deep learning model that predicts position-resolved and condition-dependent initiation landscapes. IncepTIS-guided optimization generates de novo mRNA 5' leaders with stress-responsive initiation patterns. Together, TISCA2 and IncepTIS provide an experimental and computational framework for mapping, predicting and engineering translation initiation in mammalian cells and tissues.

papers.title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the IDR of transcription factor RUNX2. We show that RUNX2 requires its C-terminal IDR to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR sequence is dispensable, and instead features of the conformational ensemble predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo. Together, these results illustrate the central role for TF IDRs in chromatin binding and extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

papers.title: Pan-cancer proteomic map of 949 human cell lines
papers.abstract: The proteome provides unique insights into disease biology beyond the genome and transcriptome. A lack of large proteomic datasets has restricted the identification of new cancer biomarkers. Here, proteomes of 949 cancer cell lines across 28 tissue types are analyzed by mass spectrometry. Deploying a workflow to quantify 8,498 proteins, these data capture evidence of cell-type and post-transcriptional modifications. Integrating multi-omics, drug response, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene essentiality screens with a deep learning-based pipeline reveals thousands of protein biomarkers of cancer vulnerabilities that are not significant at the transcript level. The power of the proteome to predict drug response is very similar to that of the transcriptome. Further, random downsampling to only 1,500 proteins has limited impact on predictive power, consistent with protein networks being highly connected and co-regulated. This pan-cancer proteomic map (ProCan-DepMapSanger) is a comprehensive resource available at https://cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk.

papers.title: Cell clustering for spatial transcriptomics data with graph neural networks
papers.abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics data can provide high-throughput gene expression profiling and spatial structure of tissues simultaneously. An essential question of its initial analysis is cell clustering. However, most existing studies rely on only gene expression information and cannot utilize spatial information efficiently. Taking advantages of two recent technical development, spatial transcriptomics and graph neural network, we thus introduce CCST, Cell Clustering for Spatial Transcriptomics data with graph neural network, an unsupervised cell clustering method based on graph convolutional network to improve ab initio cell clustering and discovering of novel sub cell types based on curated cell category annotation. CCST is a general framework for dealing with various kinds of spatially resolved transcriptomics. With application to five in vitro and in vivo spatial datasets, we show that CCST outperforms other spatial cluster approaches on spatial transcriptomics datasets, and can clearly identify all four cell cycle phases from MERFISH data of cultured cells, and find novel functional sub cell types with different micro-environments from seqFISH+ data of brain, which are all validated experimentally, inspiring novel biological hypotheses about the underlying interactions among cell state, cell type and micro-environment.

papers.title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
papers.abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

papers.title: DeepHel: improving the accuracy and completeness of Helitron annotation with a multi-stage deep learning framework.
papers.abstract: Accurate and comprehensive annotation of Helitrons remains challenging due to weak structural signals, ambiguous termini, sequence fragmentation, and complex nested insertions. Existing methods often exhibit limited sensitivity, high false-positive rates, and insufficient support for simultaneous detection of both HLE1 and HLE2, leading to incomplete and imprecise annotation. We present DeepHel, a multi-stage deep learning framework that improves the accuracy and completeness of Helitron annotation by modeling intactness, boundary characteristic, and structural consistency. DeepHel formulates Helitron detection as a staged representation learning problem, integrating sequence features, structural signals, and multiple sequence alignment information across four coordinated modules: candidate identification, intact element recognition, boundary refinement, and Helitron classification, followed by nested insertion removal. Benchmarking across five eukaryotic genomes under three evaluation settings demonstrates that DeepHel achieves a superior balance between sensitivity and precision compared with existing tools, including HiTE, HELIANO, HelitronScanner, RepeatModeler2, and EDTA. In particular, DeepHel improves the recovery of intact Helitron families (completeness), while maintaining robust performance in challenging scenarios such as low-copy elements and genomes with complex nested insertions. Furthermore, DeepHel identifies previously unannotated Helitrons with well-defined structural features, providing additional insights into Helitron diversity and genome organization. These results show that DeepHel provides a robust and comprehensive solution for accurate and complete annotation of both HLE1 and HLE2 across diverse eukaryotic genomes. DeepHel is freely available at Github: https://github.com/lyysxb/DeepHel, with the archived version at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/22069775.

papers.title: scDeepSim: Deep Generative Simulation for Controlled Benchmarking of Single-Cell Methods
papers.abstract: Benchmarking single-cell computational methods requires both realistic data and reliable ground truth. However, annotating real datasets is costly and, even when available, may not fully represent the diverse settings where methods are used. Simulators address this gap by generating synthetic data that has fully specified ground truth and whose structure can be tailored to challenge competing methods. Existing single-cell simulators can broadly be divided into statistical and deep generative classes. Statistical simulators offer interpretable parameters for controlling simulated data, but their modeling assumptions may not accurately represent real data. Deep generative models can learn complex expression patterns, but it remains unclear how to transparently control individual biological or technical factors without introducing unintended effects. We introduce scDeepSim, a simulator that combines a structured variational autoencoder with latent diffusion to generate synthetic single-cell expression profiles. It allows users to intervene on selected biological or technical factors at user-specified strengths, producing realistic datasets with benchmark ground truth. We demonstrate this capability by benchmarking batch correction and trajectory inference methods, showing how batch-effect strength affects batch mixing and cell-type preservation, and how trajectory geometry and noise affect pseudotime recovery. scDeepSim therefore enables researchers to vary selected biological and technical factors in realistic simulated data and assess how these changes affect the performance of single-cell analysis methods, helping understand when such methods may be appropriately applied. Code for the scDeepSim simulator and experiments is available at https://github.com/LangtianM/scDeepSim.

papers.title: A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain
papers.abstract: Abstract The human brain contains an extraordinarily diverse set of neuronal and glial cell types. Recent advances in single cell transcriptomics have begun to delineate the cellular heterogeneity in different brain regions, but the transcriptional regulatory programs responsible for the identity and function of each brain cell type remain to be defined. Here, we carried out single nucleus ATAC-seq analysis to probe the open chromatin landscape from over 1.1 million cells in 42 brain regions of three neurotypical adult donors. Integrative analysis of the resulting data identified 107 distinct cell types and revealed the cell-type-specific usage of 544,735 candidate cis-regulatory DNA elements (cCREs) in the human genome. Nearly 1/3 of them displayed sequence conservation as well as chromatin accessibility in the mouse brain. On the other hand, nearly 40% cCREs were human specific, with chromatin accessibility associated with species-restricted gene expression. Interestingly, these human specific cCREs were enriched for distinct families of retrotransposable elements, which displayed cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility. We uncovered strong associations between specific brain cell types and neuropsychiatric disorders. We futher developed deep learning models to predict regulatory function of non-coding disease risk variants.

papers.title: Identification of gene kinetics patterns improves RNA velocity and cell fate prediction using JuloVelo
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA velocity has transformed our capacity to predict future cell states from sequencing snapshots, but existing methods rely on constant or binary kinetic assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneous splicing dynamics of cellular differentiation. Here we present JuloVelo, a deep learning framework that demonstrates that identifying gene kinetics patterns to initialize neural network training dramatically improves RNA velocity model performance. By pre-determining whether each gene follows a Circle, Complete induction, or Complete repression pattern across cellular differentiation, JuloVelo initializes training with pattern-matched, pre-trained network weights, effectively guiding the cell-specific kinetics optimization away from biologically implausible parameter regimes. Additionally, JuloVelo demonstrates that multiome datasets can also be processed and modeled by utilizing promoter chromatin accessibility to guide kinetics pre-determination, and integrates an in silico perturbation framework to simulate transcription factor modulation on cell fate. Validated across eight datasets spanning erythrogenesis, neurogenesis, and endocrinogenesis, JuloVelo consistently outperformed constant-rate and cell-specific models, resolving the entire five-lineage differentiation program in hippocampal neurogenesis. Multiome processing improved both intrinsic and extrinsic velocity stability, and JuloVelo reduced computational execution time by approximately 70% compared to cellDancer. JuloVelo is available as an open-source package at https://github.com/jhlabtw/JuloVelo.jl.

papers.title: A benchmark study of deep learning-based multi-omics data fusion methods for cancer
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: A fused method using a combination of multi-omics data enables a comprehensive study of complex biological processes and highlights the interrelationship of relevant biomolecules and their functions. Driven by high-throughput sequencing technologies, several promising deep learning methods have been proposed for fusing multi-omics data generated from a large number of samples. RESULTS: In this study, 16 representative deep learning methods are comprehensively evaluated on simulated, single-cell, and cancer multi-omics datasets. For each of the datasets, two tasks are designed: classification and clustering. The classification performance is evaluated by using three benchmarking metrics including accuracy, F1 macro, and F1 weighted. Meanwhile, the clustering performance is evaluated by using four benchmarking metrics including the Jaccard index (JI), C-index, silhouette score, and Davies Bouldin score. For the cancer multi-omics datasets, the methods' strength in capturing the association of multi-omics dimensionality reduction results with survival and clinical annotations is further evaluated. The benchmarking results indicate that moGAT achieves the best classification performance. Meanwhile, efmmdVAE, efVAE, and lfmmdVAE show the most promising performance across all complementary contexts in clustering tasks. CONCLUSIONS: Our benchmarking results not only provide a reference for biomedical researchers to choose appropriate deep learning-based multi-omics data fusion methods, but also suggest the future directions for the development of more effective multi-omics data fusion methods. The deep learning frameworks are available at https://github.com/zhenglinyi/DL-mo .

papers.title: AdaGeneBudget: Cell-Adaptive Gene-Token Allocation for Efficient Single-Cell Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) represent each cell using sequences of gene-associated tokens, making embedding extraction increasingly costly as the number of cells and expressed genes grows. Existing input policies typically rely on fixed input budgets, with retained genes determined by random subsampling, model-native ranking, or a dataset-level highly variable gene (HVG) panel. However, they do not jointly determine, for each cell, which genes to retain and how many tokens to allocate. We introduce AdaGeneBudget, a training-free gene-token selection method that combines each gene's expression with reference-derived inverse detection frequency and retains the shortest ranked prefix that captures a target fraction of the cell's expression-specificity score mass. The resulting cell-specific budget is bounded by minimum and maximum lengths, requires no cell-type labels, and leaves the pretrained backbone unchanged. We evaluated AdaGeneBudget in a frozen-backbone inference setting using pretrained scGPT and Geneformer models on Kang and PBMC reference-mapping tasks, with an additional scPRINT comparison against its official HVG policy and an expressed-only HVG control. Across four scGPT and Geneformer backbone-dataset pairs, AdaGeneBudget substantially reduced mean gene-token counts and peak GPU memory while increasing embedding-extraction throughput by up to 4.63x. Despite this compression, it preserved native-level aggregate annotation utility and numerically outperformed token-matched random and Top-Expression baselines. AdaGeneBudget also preserved fine-grained and low-support cell identities and retained lineage-marker programs and stimulation-associated pathway genes under compression. In scPRINT, both HVG controls achieved higher annotation macro-F1, whereas AdaGeneBudget more faithfully preserved the stimulation-induced embedding direction. These results establish biologically informed, cell-adaptive gene-token allocation as a practical complement to architectural and systems-level efficiency methods for applying existing scFMs to new datasets. They also suggest that cell-adaptive input allocation may be a useful design principle for future models operating under finite token budgets.

papers.title: A mixture-of-experts deep generative model for integrated analysis of single-cell multiomics data
papers.abstract: The recent development of single-cell multiomics analysis has enabled simultaneous detection of multiple traits at the single-cell level, providing deeper insights into cellular phenotypes and functions in diverse tissues. However, currently, it is challenging to infer the joint representations and learn relationships among multiple modalities from complex multimodal single-cell data. Here, we present scMM, a novel deep generative model-based framework for the extraction of interpretable joint representations and crossmodal generation. scMM addresses the complexity of data by leveraging a mixture-of-experts multimodal variational autoencoder. The pseudocell generation strategy of scMM compensates for the limited interpretability of deep learning models, and the proposed approach experimentally discovered multimodal regulatory programs associated with latent dimensions. Analysis of recently produced datasets validated that scMM facilitates high-resolution clustering with rich interpretability. Furthermore, we show that crossmodal generation by scMM leads to more precise prediction and data integration compared with the state-of-the-art and conventional approaches.

papers.title: scGNN is a novel graph neural network framework for single-cell RNA-Seq analyses
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-Seq) is widely used to reveal the heterogeneity and dynamics of tissues, organisms, and complex diseases, but its analyses still suffer from multiple grand challenges, including the sequencing sparsity and complex differential patterns in gene expression. We introduce the scGNN (single-cell graph neural network) to provide a hypothesis-free deep learning framework for scRNA-Seq analyses. This framework formulates and aggregates cell-cell relationships with graph neural networks and models heterogeneous gene expression patterns using a left-truncated mixture Gaussian model. scGNN integrates three iterative multi-modal autoencoders and outperforms existing tools for gene imputation and cell clustering on four benchmark scRNA-Seq datasets. In an Alzheimer's disease study with 13,214 single nuclei from postmortem brain tissues, scGNN successfully illustrated disease-related neural development and the differential mechanism. scGNN provides an effective representation of gene expression and cell-cell relationships. It is also a powerful framework that can be applied to general scRNA-Seq analyses.

papers.title: Genome-wide prediction of disease variant effects with a deep protein language model
papers.abstract: Predicting the effects of coding variants is a major challenge. While recent deep-learning models have improved variant effect prediction accuracy, they cannot analyze all coding variants due to dependency on close homologs or software limitations. Here we developed a workflow using ESM1b, a 650-million-parameter protein language model, to predict all ~450 million possible missense variant effects in the human genome, and made all predictions available on a web portal. ESM1b outperformed existing methods in classifying ~150,000 ClinVar/HGMD missense variants as pathogenic or benign and predicting measurements across 28 deep mutational scan datasets. We further annotated ~2 million variants as damaging only in specific protein isoforms, demonstrating the importance of considering all isoforms when predicting variant effects. Our approach also generalizes to more complex coding variants such as in-frame indels and stop-gains. Together, these results establish protein language models as an effective, accurate and general approach to predicting variant effects.

papers.title: Single-cell spatial landscapes of the lung tumour immune microenvironment
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-cell technologies have revealed the complexity of the tumour immune microenvironment with unparalleled resolution 1–9 . Most clinical strategies rely on histopathological stratification of tumour subtypes, yet the spatial context of single-cell phenotypes within these stratified subgroups is poorly understood. Here we apply imaging mass cytometry to characterize the tumour and immunological landscape of samples from 416 patients with lung adenocarcinoma across five histological patterns. We resolve more than 1.6 million cells, enabling spatial analysis of immune lineages and activation states with distinct clinical correlates, including survival. Using deep learning, we can predict with high accuracy those patients who will progress after surgery using a single 1-mm 2 tumour core, which could be informative for clinical management following surgical resection. Our dataset represents a valuable resource for the non-small cell lung cancer research community and exemplifies the utility of spatial resolution within single-cell analyses. This study also highlights how artificial intelligence can improve our understanding of microenvironmental features that underlie cancer progression and may influence future clinical practice.

papers.title: DeepTTA: a transformer-based model for predicting cancer drug response
papers.abstract: Identifying new lead molecules to treat cancer requires more than a decade of dedicated effort. Before selected drug candidates are used in the clinic, their anti-cancer activity is generally validated by in vitro cellular experiments. Therefore, accurate prediction of cancer drug response is a critical and challenging task for anti-cancer drugs design and precision medicine. With the development of pharmacogenomics, the combination of efficient drug feature extraction methods and omics data has made it possible to use computational models to assist in drug response prediction. In this study, we propose DeepTTA, a novel end-to-end deep learning model that utilizes transformer for drug representation learning and a multilayer neural network for transcriptomic data prediction of the anti-cancer drug responses. Specifically, DeepTTA uses transcriptomic gene expression data and chemical substructures of drugs for drug response prediction. Compared to existing methods, DeepTTA achieved higher performance in terms of root mean square error, Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient on multiple test sets. Moreover, we discovered that anti-cancer drugs bortezomib and dactinomycin provide a potential therapeutic option with multiple clinical indications. With its excellent performance, DeepTTA is expected to be an effective method in cancer drug design.

papers.title: Identification of driver genes for critical forms of COVID-19 in a deeply phenotyped young patient cohort
papers.abstract: Abstract The etiopathogenesis of severe COVID-19 remains unknown. Indeed given major confounding factors (age and co-morbidities), true drivers of this condition have remained elusive. Here, we employ an unprecedented multi-omics analysis, combined with artificial intelligence, in a young patient cohort where major co-morbidities have been excluded at the onset. Here, we established a three-tier cohort of individuals younger than 50 years without major comorbidities. These included 47 “critical” (in the ICU under mechanical ventilation) and 25 “non-critical” (in a noncritical care ward) COVID-19 patients as well as 22 healthy individuals. The analyses included whole-genome sequencing, whole-blood RNA sequencing, plasma and blood mononuclear cells proteomics, cytokine profiling and high-throughput immunophenotyping. An ensemble of machine learning, deep learning, quantum annealing and structural causal modeling led to key findings. Critical patients were characterized by exacerbated inflammation, perturbed lymphoid/myeloid compartments, coagulation and viral cell biology. Within a unique gene signature that differentiated critical from noncritical patients, several driver genes promoted severe COVID-19 among which the upregulated metalloprotease ADAM9 was key. This gene signature was replicated in an independent cohort of 81 critical and 73 recovered COVID-19 patients, as were ADAM9 transcripts, soluble form and proteolytic activity. Ex vivo ADAM9 inhibition affected SARS-CoV-2 uptake and replication in human lung epithelial cells. In conclusion, within a young, otherwise healthy, COVID-19 cohort, we provide the landscape of biological perturbations in vivo where a unique gene signature differentiated critical from non-critical patients. The key driver, ADAM9 , interfered with SARS-CoV-2 biology. A repositioning strategy for anti-ADAM9 therapeutic is feasible. One sentence summary Etiopathogenesis of severe COVID19 in a young patient population devoid of comorbidities.

papers.title: Interpretable deep learning translation of GWAS and multi-omics findings to identify pathobiology and drug repurposing in Alzheimer’s disease
papers.abstract: Abstract Human genome sequencing studies have identified numerous loci associated with complex diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Translating human genetic findings (i.e., genome-wide association studies [GWAS]) to pathobiology and therapeutic discovery, however, remains a major challenge. To address this critical problem, we present a net work t opology-based deep learning framework to identify disease- a ssociated g enes (NETTAG). NETTAG is capable of integrating multigenomics data along with the protein-protein interactome to infer putative risk genes and drug targets impacted by GWAS loci. Specifically, we leverage non-coding GWAS loci effects on expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), histone-QTLs, and transcription factor binding-QTLs, enhancers and CpG islands, promoter regions, open chromatin, and promoter flanking regions. The key premises of NETTAG are that the disease risk genes exhibit distinct functional characteristics compared to non-risk genes and therefore can be distinguished by their aggregated genomic features under the human protein interactome. Applying NETTAG to the latest AD GWAS data, we identified 156 putative AD-risk genes (i.e., APOE , BIN1 , GSK3B , MARK4 , and PICALM ). We showed that predicted risk genes are: 1) significantly enriched in AD-related pathobiological pathways, 2) more likely to be differentially expressed regarding transcriptome and proteome of AD brains, and 3) enriched in druggable targets with approved medicines (i.e., choline and ibudilast). In summary, our findings suggest that understanding of human pathobiology and therapeutic development could benefit from a network-based deep learning methodology that utilizes GWAS findings under the multimodal genomic analyses.

papers.title: Integrate multi-omics data with biological interaction networks using Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comprehensive molecular profiling of various cancers and other diseases has generated vast amounts of multi-omics data. Each type of -omics data corresponds to one feature space, such as gene expression, miRNA expression, DNA methylation, etc. Integrating multi-omics data can link different layers of molecular feature spaces and is crucial to elucidate molecular pathways underlying various diseases. Machine learning approaches to mining multi-omics data hold great promises in uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features. However, due to the "big p, small n" problem (i.e., small sample sizes with high-dimensional features), training a large-scale generalizable deep learning model with multi-omics data alone is very challenging. RESULTS: We developed a method called Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE) with network constraints that can seamlessly integrate multi-omics data and domain knowledge such as molecular interaction networks. Our method learns feature and patient embeddings simultaneously with deep representation learning. Both feature representations and patient representations are subject to certain constraints specified as regularization terms in the training objective. By incorporating domain knowledge into the training objective, we implicitly introduced a good inductive bias into the machine learning model, which helps improve model generalizability. We performed extensive experiments on the TCGA datasets and demonstrated the power of integrating multi-omics data and biological interaction networks using our proposed method for predicting target clinical variables. CONCLUSIONS: To alleviate the overfitting problem in deep learning on multi-omics data with the "big p, small n" problem, it is helpful to incorporate biological domain knowledge into the model as inductive biases. It is very promising to design machine learning models that facilitate the seamless integration of large-scale multi-omics data and biomedical domain knowledge for uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features and clinical features.

papers.title: Deep Learning–Based Multi-Omics Integration Robustly Predicts Survival in Liver Cancer
papers.abstract: Abstract Identifying robust survival subgroups of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) will significantly improve patient care. Currently, endeavor of integrating multi-omics data to explicitly predict HCC survival from multiple patient cohorts is lacking. To fill this gap, we present a deep learning (DL)–based model on HCC that robustly differentiates survival subpopulations of patients in six cohorts. We built the DL-based, survival-sensitive model on 360 HCC patients' data using RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq), miRNA sequencing (miRNA-Seq), and methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which predicts prognosis as good as an alternative model where genomics and clinical data are both considered. This DL-based model provides two optimal subgroups of patients with significant survival differences (P = 7.13e−6) and good model fitness [concordance index (C-index) = 0.68]. More aggressive subtype is associated with frequent TP53 inactivation mutations, higher expression of stemness markers (KRT19 and EPCAM) and tumor marker BIRC5, and activated Wnt and Akt signaling pathways. We validated this multi-omics model on five external datasets of various omics types: LIRI-JP cohort (n = 230, C-index = 0.75), NCI cohort (n = 221, C-index = 0.67), Chinese cohort (n = 166, C-index = 0.69), E-TABM-36 cohort (n = 40, C-index = 0.77), and Hawaiian cohort (n = 27, C-index = 0.82). This is the first study to employ DL to identify multi-omics features linked to the differential survival of patients with HCC. Given its robustness over multiple cohorts, we expect this workflow to be useful at predicting HCC prognosis prediction. Clin Cancer Res; 24(6); 1248–59. ©2017 AACR.

papers.title: Gene Expression Nebulas 2.0: an updated resource of gene expression profiles by incorporating more datasets, annotations, and functionalities.
papers.abstract: Gene Expression Nebulas (GEN; https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gen/) is an open-access database that provides standardized transcriptomic profiles and manually curated metadata across diverse species. Compared with the previous release, the updated GEN has expanded in terms of datasets from 323 to 668, samples from 50 500 to 102 679, cells from 15 540 169 to 23 461 252, and species from 30 to 100. GEN 2.0 adds spatial transcriptomics data and disease-associated expression annotations from 82 human bulk RNA-seq datasets spanning 62 disease categories, including distinct subtypes, across 12 disease systems. In addition, it has been significantly upgraded by providing high-quality gene expression profiles for artificial intelligence applications, a web-based service to accept transcriptomic data submission, and an updated online analysis tool for gene expression comparisons across species, tissues, and diseases. Together, GEN offers more comprehensive, standardized gene expression profiles across diverse species and thus serves as a fundamental resource for uncovering molecular functional mechanisms and deciphering complex regulatory architecture.

papers.title: TFXcan reveals transcription factor programs driving GWAS loci.
papers.abstract: Disease-associated loci identified by genome-wide association studies (GWASs) may induce effects by altering transcription factor (TF) binding. However, due to the scarcity of population-level TF-binding experiments, identifying these disrupted TFs remains challenging. To address this, we present the TFXcan framework, which correlates genetically predicted TF binding with phenotypes to nominate TF-tissue pairs that may regulate complex traits. Within this framework, we introduce Enpact, a deep learning-based approach that integrates Enformer and IMPACT to infer personalized TF-binding events. Leveraging Enpact, we correlate predicted binding profiles for 700 TF-tissue pairs with prostate cancer risk, identifying multiple implicated TFs at risk loci. Matrix decomposition further reveals clusters of TF-tissue pairs, termed "programs," acting as candidate drivers of disease risk. TFXcan represents the first method capable of predicting TF binding from genotype data at scale, enabling systematic identification of TFs and regulatory programs underlying complex traits.

papers.title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models.
papers.abstract: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from Cα-only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.
papers.venue: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

papers.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation.
papers.abstract: Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology1,2. Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes1,3,4. However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

papers.title: stem.MAP: Identification of cell-type-specific protein complexes in mammalian embryonic stem cells.
papers.abstract: Protein complexes carry out critical functions during development. Mapping cell-type-specific protein complexes in early embryogenesis is essential for uncovering the molecular mechanisms of embryonic development. We unfortunately currently lack a catalog of protein complexes specific for embryogenesis including embryonic stem cells. Here we develop a proteomics-based machine learning workflow to predict protein complexes present in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC). Our method integrates data from a cell-type agnostic protein complex resource with co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS) experiments on mESC. Our resource, stem.MAP, identifies 3,986 complexes encompassing ~133,000 unique interactions, and 8,616 proteins. stem.MAP captures variant complexes critical for stem cell function including the PRC2, BAF and NuRD complexes. stem.MAP also discriminates mutually exclusive interactions specific to embryonic stem cells (e.g. Eif4ebp2 - Eif4e). Finally we observe 1,388 high confidence stem.MAP interactions found only in mESC CF-MS data, many with support from AlphaFold modeling and a gastruloid coregulation network. We make stem.MAP protein complexes available through our web resource: stem.proteincomplexes.org. We anticipate stem.MAP will be beneficial to the study of early development and we expect our proteomics-based machine learning workflow to be applicable to the creation of any context-specific protein interaction network.

papers.title: Contrastive Learning Improves Generalization on M2OR Olfactory Binding Dataset
papers.abstract: Olfaction-based biosensors stand to have profound impacts in fields such as medical diagnostics, national security, and drug discovery. A promising mode of vapor phase biodetection mimics volatile organic compound-olfactory receptor (VOC-OR) interactions with target-specific protein or peptide probes; however, lack of experimental coverage remains a core bottleneck. Current computational approaches aim to improve prediction of VOC-OR binding to reduce experimental burden, and current machine learning approaches fail to demonstrate a level of generalization that addresses current engineering challenges. Here, using the Molecular to Olfactory Dataset (M2OR) and Insect Olfactory Binding Protein Database (iOBPdb) datasets, data partitioning methods and their performance are evaluated on a neural network and contrastive learning framework on such VOC-OR binding datasets, varying: model training, architecture, and structure of the input data distribution. It was found that holding out certain chemical or proteomic motifs from the training data diminished model performance with a two layer neural network model. The model was able to generalize to state of the art performance (0.88 AUCROC) on every data split by applying a contrastive learning objective defined by shared molecular constituents and a stochastic sampler. This suggests the contrastive objective provides a strong inductive bias for neural networks to predict novel VOC-OR pairs. These findings highlight that model performance on pairwise biological interaction datasets can be inflated through identity leakage from constituent overlap, and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we show contrastive regularization mitigates dataset degeneracy through enforcement of compatibility in the models latent geometry that may extend to other binder target-datasets where identity leakage confounds evaluation.

papers.title: StableProt: Structure-Aware Deep Learning for Protein Thermostability (Tm) and Environmental Adaptation (OGT) Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting protein melting temperature (Tm) and organismal optimal growth temperature (OGT) is essential for enzyme engineering, biocatalyst design, and metagenomic bioprospecting, yet computational prediction faces several fundamental bottlenecks: sequence-only representations miss tertiary packing; dual-task coupling induces destructive gradient conflict; natural database skew (>87% mesophiles) drives mesophilic collapse; and existing tools produce uncalibrated point predictions. To address these challenges, we present StableProt, a structure-aware framework that couples amino acid sequences with Foldseek 3Di structural tokens via a frozen SaProt backbone to capture 3D contacts. Disjoint heads condition thermodynamic stability on ecological context without gradient conflict, while targeted 14% mesophilic subsampling expands thermophile representation to eliminate mesophilic collapse. Calibrated ensemble modeling reduces calibration error to 1.92%, providing dependable 95% confidence intervals. Evaluating models across 10{degrees}C temperature intervals reveals severe baseline collapse at thermal extremes, whereas StableProt maintains robust accuracy across regimes. On ProThermDB and zero-shot FireProtDB, StableProt achieves state-of-the-art probabilistic accuracy (CRPS = 4.52{degrees}C and 8.71{degrees}C) while recovering 92.0% of hyperthermophiles ([≥]80{degrees}C), and in prospective validation, its calibrated intervals capture both enzyme stability (75.3% coverage) and host environmental growth temperatures (78.1% coverage). StableProt is freely accessible as an interactive web server at https://stableprot.dixitlab.org/.

papers.title: All-Atom Structure Tokenizer: AtomLM-9b for Biomolecular Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction.

papers.title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
papers.abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG's 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.

papers.title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
